title: From screen to interaction: adult–child engagement with play school, 60 years on
text_snippet: From screen to interaction: adult–child engagement with play school, 60 years on Abstract In 2026, Play School marks 60 years as a foundational Australian children’s program, offering a timely moment to reconsider its role in supporting early literacy and adult–child interaction. This paper investigates how co‑viewing Play School episodes creates opportunities for meaningful engagement between young children aged under five years and their accompanying adults. By identifying specific segments within episodes and analysing the interactional possibilities embedded in them, the paper explores how children respond to the program and how adults mediate these responses to foster participation, meaning-making, and early literacy practices. Observations highlight the significance of decision‑making, agency, shared enjoyment, and embodied engagement—including movement and play—as central features of the co‑viewing experience. These findings demonstrate that Play School’s distinctive interactive design continues to invite conversational turn‑taking, joint attention, and language-rich exchanges that align with contemporary understandings of early literacy development. title: Representations of guided writing in system-developed curriculum materials: a study from New South Wales and Victoria
text_snippet: Representations of guided writing in system-developed curriculum materials: a study from New South Wales and Victoria Abstract Concerns about declining student writing outcomes in Australia have led to some state governments investing in system-developed English curriculum materials. While these materials aim to promote consistency and alignment with ‘evidence-informed’ practice across classrooms, less is known about how writing pedagogies, such as guided writing, are being represented within them. Using a qualitative research design, two Stage 3 persuasive writing units developed by the New South Wales and Victorian Departments of Education are explored. A 5W Framework for Guided Writing is used as a purpose-built analytical tool to explore where guided writing is positioned, why it is implemented, when it occurs, who directs the practice, and what forms of writing are produced. Findings indicate that guided writing is inconsistently embedded across lesson sequences and frequently represented as a fragmented, skill-focused activity rather than a collaborative support for extended text construction. title: Policy, pedagogy and curriculum in the teaching of reading in early years classrooms in Australia: A Narrative Literature Review (2004–2025)
text_snippet: Policy, pedagogy and curriculum in the teaching of reading in early years classrooms in Australia: A Narrative Literature Review (2004–2025) Abstract In this narrative literature review we trace shifts in reading policy and pedagogy in the early years of Australian primary education from 2004 to 2025. Anchored in Teaching Reading: Report and Recommendations by Ken Rowe, we map changes that reshaped how reading is defined and taught in Foundation to Year 3 classrooms in New South Wales, Queensland, and Victoria. The review eschews a phonics versus whole language binary by adopting Bingham and Hall-Kenyon’s continuum of pedagogical orientations, with skills-focused instruction at one anchor, whole language at the other, and balanced literacy in between. It synthesises research literature and analyses state and national curriculum documents. Across jurisdictions, the centre of gravity has shifted toward systematic phonics mandates, while attention to meaning, sociocultural, and critical dimensions narrows, even though a balanced approach remains strong in policy and curriculum. The review examines consequences for professional judgement, teacher trust, and accountability, noting that polarised positions understate the complexity of reading development. title: The architecture of crisis: problematising a global ban on the three-cueing system in reading education
text_snippet: The architecture of crisis: problematising a global ban on the three-cueing system in reading education Abstract Contemporary literacy policy is increasingly shaped by crisis narratives that position reading achievement as a problem requiring urgent intervention. This paper examines the growing movement to ban or discredit the three-cueing system in reading education through an analysis of contemporary policy discourse in the United States. Drawing on Carol Bacchi’s framework for analysing problem representations in policy, we investigate how legislation and public commentary aligned with the Science of Reading (SoR) construct three-cueing as a harmful instructional practice that should be removed from classrooms. Using an Alabama news report on Alabama Senate Bill 168, we identify the assumptions, silences, and effects embedded within this representation of the problem. The analysis shows that three-cueing is frequently conflated with guessing from pictures or context and positioned as incompatible with scientific evidence, despite ongoing debate about its purpose, interpretation, and role in reading. title: Engaging reading: A structured pedagogical framework for teaching reading for enjoyment (RfE) as educative practice in primary English classrooms
text_snippet: Engaging reading: A structured pedagogical framework for teaching reading for enjoyment (RfE) as educative practice in primary English classrooms Abstract Decades of research consistently demonstrate that student engagement in reading for enjoyment (RfE) is strongly associated with a wide range of educational benefits. Well-documented benefits include gains in reading achievement and improvements in students’ reading attitudes, motivation, and confidence. In Australia, engagement with texts for enjoyment is explicitly articulated as a curriculum expectation. Contemporary literacy policy, however, prioritises some aspects of reading instruction, while those related to RfE receive comparatively less systematic attention. As a result, classroom support for RfE is often constrained by policy settings, narrow pedagogical emphases, and fragmented practices. This article addresses a specific and persistent challenge within this broader context: the absence of coherent pedagogical structures and shared policy language to support the intentional teaching of RfE. Drawing on a doctoral narrative inquiry with four primary teachers, and informed by John Dewey’s (1934) seminal aesthetic theory, the article introduces an original conceptual pedagogical framework designed to support the teaching of RfE in the primary English classroom. title: Shared book reading and the home literacy environment: a worldwide study using Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library
text_snippet: Shared book reading and the home literacy environment: a worldwide study using Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library Abstract We investigated the impact of Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, a program that distributes age-appropriate books monthly to children from birth to age five, on the home literacy environment (HLE). Caregivers enrolled in the program in the United States, Australia, Canada, the Republic of Ireland, and the United Kingdom completed surveys at three time points: (1) prior to receiving any books (baseline survey; n = 86,206); (2) six months after the baseline survey (survey 2; n = 35,435); and (3) six months after survey 2 (survey 3; n = 18,112). The HLE was assessed using items that asked about the frequency and duration of shared book reading, the number of children’s books in the home, and the child's age when shared book reading began. Responses from caregivers who completed all three surveys ( n = 18,112; Imagination Library group) were compared to those in a comparison group who had completed the baseline survey but had not yet received any books ( n = 37,776). title: Children becoming readers, writers, or both? Caregiver perspectives on connections and imbalances in children’s reading and writing identities
text_snippet: Children becoming readers, writers, or both? Caregiver perspectives on connections and imbalances in children’s reading and writing identities Abstract This study examines the interrelationship of reading and writing in elementary grade children through an identity perspective to explore children’s broader processes of literacy learning and becoming in a climate where reading and writing instruction are not consistently given equal attention. Attention to identities opens space for complexity in the reading-writing dynamic and for considering the simultaneous development of children as readers and writers. This qualitative study uses interviews with caregivers in the United States to collect information on children’s reading and writing identities across grades K-5. A content analysis of the interviews was guided by thematic analysis to explore possible connections and imbalances in children’s reading and writing development. Findings provide insights into emerging differences in children’s reading and writing identities in the elementary grades, and the potential impacts of these differences on children’s trajectories as readers and writers. title: Teacher autonomy: the impact of evidence-based practices and social validity
text_snippet: Teacher autonomy: the impact of evidence-based practices and social validity Abstract The use of evidence-based practices (EBP) in education has grown significantly over recent decades, with demonstrated positive impact on student outcomes. However, concerns have been raised about the potential negative consequences of mandated EBPs eroding teacher autonomy, particularly when driven by top-down policy directives. Despite growing debate, limited empirical research has explored how teachers navigate this tension between external mandates and teacher professional autonomy. This study investigates how teachers in Australia perceive their autonomy regarding implementing mandated EBPs in literacy education, with particular attention to the social validity they assign to these practices. A survey of 78 teachers evaluated both their valuation of EBPs and their perceived autonomy, followed by semi-structured interviews with two participants. Results suggested a positive relationship between teachers’ social validation of EBPs and their perceived autonomy, while the thematic analysis of interview data revealed a more contextually grounded picture that highlighted the varied lived experiences situated beneath this broader pattern. title: The ‘how long’ question: EAL students’ progression through phases of English language development in Australian schools
text_snippet: The ‘how long’ question: EAL students’ progression through phases of English language development in Australian schools Abstract This article addresses the question of how long it takes students who are learning English as an additional language (EAL) in the Australian context to develop the level of English necessary for equitable participation in the curriculum. Extensive previous international research has investigated this question, however, except for one study, little relevant research has taken place in Australia. In response to this gap, this article presents outcomes from a large-scale research project undertaken in collaboration with the NSW Department of Education. The project involved analysis of two major sets of data: students’ NAPLAN test results over a period of 9 years, and teachers’ judgements of their EAL students’ progression, using the national EAL/D Learning Progression (Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority, 2015), also over 9 years. This article addresses the outcomes and implications from analysis of the teacher judgements, while outcomes from the NAPLAN analysis are reported elsewhere (Lu, Hammond et al., 2025b). title: Investigating links between early instrumental learning and literacy skills development
text_snippet: Investigating links between early instrumental learning and literacy skills development Abstract Australian national authorities set clear reading competency goals during primary education. The development of reading skills and music training has been linked, with research over the past 15 years reporting improvements in phonological awareness through music interventions. This study investigated such links between instrumental music learning, its duration, and specific reading skills. We administered reading tests to Year 3–Year 6 students and analysed the outcomes against instrumental learning data. The results show advantages for music students in Years 3–4 in one reading category and stronger outcomes for music students in Years 5–6 in four categories versus control. Our findings demonstrate a link between the duration of instrumental learning and development of reading skills, highlighting a benefit from providing early and sustained opportunities for instrumental music learning to all primary age children to support the development of their literacy skills.

title: Dialogism for democracy: reimagining argumentation in English curriculum
text_snippet: Dialogism for democracy: reimagining argumentation in English curriculum Abstract In response to mounting political polarisation and a weakening of civic discourse, there is growing recognition—both in Australia and internationally—of the need to cultivate empathy, perspective-taking, and ethical engagement with difference. This paper argues that subject English is uniquely positioned to support these aims, not only due to its mandated curricular status, but also through its long-standing civic mission to foster democratic citizenship. Drawing on Mikhail Bakhtin’s theory of dialogism, the paper distinguishes between monologic and dialogic forms of argumentation, framing the latter as more responsive to democratic imperatives. This paper considers the writing curriculum—specifically argumentation and point-of-view composition—as a critical site for developing dialogic dispositions. Taking the Victorian Certificate of Education (VCE) English curriculum as a case study, it investigates the affordances of curriculum in fostering dialogic negotiation of conflict rather than adversarial persuasion and a finalised stance. title: Using cross-cultural picturebooks with young children to learn about values: a participative arts-based approach
text_snippet: Using cross-cultural picturebooks with young children to learn about values: a participative arts-based approach Abstract Values education is an important part of learning across the globe. This research is a qualitative case study that examined shared reading of eight theme-identified picturebooks in an early years setting to determine young children’s understanding and discussion of values. The study used Australian and Chinese picturebooks to discuss children’s understanding of values. The paper examines children’s understanding through the lens of a value-based pedagogical practice to highlight the benefits of using picturebooks as the basis for a values discussion with young children. The results showed the children clearly demonstrated an understanding of the picturebooks’ characters and even their motivations for doing things. They were also able to talk about the picturebooks by making connections to their own lives. Implications for teachers are also shared, with a focus on supporting them to provide space for children to engage with picturebooks fron different cultural context to learn about values.

title: Exploring pre-service teachers’ perceptions about their linguistic knowledge: implications for initial teacher education
text_snippet: Exploring pre-service teachers’ perceptions about their linguistic knowledge: implications for initial teacher education Abstract In the global north and south many classrooms are described as super-diverse (Vertovec, 2007) and although unevenly distributed, this is also a characteristic of many Australian classrooms. In Australia, an increasingly significant number of plurilingual people are preparing to teach in Australian classrooms, yet the voices of plurilingual Pre-Service Teachers are rarely heard. In this manuscript, we present the perceptions of a group of 28 plurilingual pre-service teachers enrolled in Initial Teacher Education (ITE) contexts in two metropolitan universities in Sydney, Australia. We analyse their perceptions of their own linguistic strengths, knowledge and experience, and their reflections on how their linguistic knowledge has been taken up in their university ITE programs and how it may inform their future teaching. Looking through a participatory social justice lens (Fraser, 2005), we analyse how the current educational landscape is informing our participants’ views and facilitating participatory justice for linguistically diverse teachers and students.

title: Multimodal practices in early English language education: a Finnish classroom case study
text_snippet: Multimodal practices in early English language education: a Finnish classroom case study Abstract This study examined how a Finnish primary school teacher implemented and navigated different modalities within a multiliteracies framework when teaching English to young learners. Finland’s recent reforms introduced foreign language learning in the first grade of primary school and established multiliteracy as a cross-curricular competence, creating an authentic context for using different modalities in language education. Employing a qualitative case study design, the data comprised survey and interview responses, a teacher‑generated multimodal diary consisting of photographs and written reflections, as well as notes, sketchnotes, and video and audio recordings of English lessons. To reflect the multimodal nature of both teaching and data collection, the analysis employed Multimodal Content Analysis. The findings indicated that the teacher employed all eight modalities: spoken and written language, visual, audio, gestural, tactile and spatial representation, and representation of oneself. title: Countering deficit narratives with translanguaging – the Australian research context
text_snippet: Countering deficit narratives with translanguaging – the Australian research context Abstract Multilingualism, plurilingualism and translanguaging are terms commonly used by applied linguists and those involved in educational attainment in Australia. They are also fields of research which attract researcher attention throughout the academic world. This paper is a scoping review of 52 papers reporting on research, theorizing and practice in Australia. The authors looked at research conducted in Australian classrooms since 2000 and aligned each of these papers to three inductive themes: culturally sustaining pedagogies, multiliteracies, and linguistic framing. The largest group of researcher papers are under the culturally sustaining pedagogies theme and it is argued in the paper that this research interest is driven by the goal for equity and quality schooling outcomes for refugee, multilingual and Indigenous learners in Australian schools. The paper asks questions about engaging with policy makers and considering English language learners’ needs in a more nuanced manner.

title: Critical thinking, oral language, and embodiment in the primary classroom: a critical thematic literature review
text_snippet: Critical thinking, oral language, and embodiment in the primary classroom: a critical thematic literature review Abstract This article presents a critical thematic literature review examining how contemporary Western research conceptualises the intersections of oracy, embodiment, power relations, oral literacies, and critical thinking in primary literacy education. Analysing peer-reviewed studies published between 2010 and 2025, and informed by longstanding Australian and international scholarship, the review identifies four major themes concerning the role of oral language and talk in literacy learning: dialogic teaching and classroom talk; critical literacy and power relations; twenty-first-century skills and educational policy; and embodied learning and multimodal literacies. A central finding is a persistent tendency to marginalise the body-in-context within dominant conceptions of oral literacy, with talk commonly framed as primarily cognitive, linguistic, or skill-based rather than embodied, relational, and situated. title: Countering deficit framings of migrant and refugee students’ language and literacy practices in Australia
text_snippet: Countering deficit framings of migrant and refugee students’ language and literacy practices in Australia Abstract The privileging of English in language and literacy education is rooted in colonial legacies that have historically marginalised Indigenous and migrant languages and knowledge systems, framing them as barriers rather than assets. Reframing literacy education requires shifting from deficit thinking to pedagogies that value students’ plurilingual repertoires, worldviews, and ecological relationships. This Special Issue explores how language and literacy education can move beyond monolingual norms to embrace plurilingual approaches that recognise and value the language and literacy practices and resources of migrant and refugee students across all levels of education. It seeks to challenge the persistent deficit discourses that frame these students’ language and literacy practices as inadequate or lacking compared to dominant English-based standards.

title: Multilingual migrant families’ equal capacity to participate in their children’s education: the benefits of activating home languages in Australian schooling
text_snippet: Multilingual migrant families’ equal capacity to participate in their children’s education: the benefits of activating home languages in Australian schooling Abstract This paper foregrounds the experiences of multilingual families in Australian schooling and their capacity to contribute significantly to their children’s education through a research-informed home language intervention. For many migrant parents, especially those on temporary skilled employment visas, concerns about English and the unfamiliar school curriculum can lead to a sense of being ill-equipped to assist their children and leaving schooling to the teachers as experts. For Education Departments and schools, however, parental involvement is seen as a sign of connection and interest. These misalignments can position migrant families as disinterested or lacking capacity to engage in their children’s schooling. However, such deficit framings are misrepresentative as migrant parents care deeply about their children’s education. This paper reports on a design-based research intervention at a rural secondary school with growing EAL/D student enrolments. title: Storytelling and literacy practices in community - bringing together place, people and texts
text_snippet: Storytelling and literacy practices in community - bringing together place, people and texts Abstract Community-based literacy research frequently positions storytelling and children’s literature as powerful sites for engaging learners in culturally responsive and critical literacy practices. This scoping review synthesises both professional and peer-reviewed research studies published between 2015 and 2025 to examine how such practices are enacted through relationships between schools, families, and communities across a variety of contexts. Analysis of 14 studies revealed that literacy learning is most commonly framed as relational and contextually situated, with storytelling functioning as a shared practice where identity and agency are negotiated. Across the literature, literacy practices and texts functioned as relational artefacts embedded within community life, rather than as standalone physical or symbolic resources. However, the review highlights a persistent limitation: while community-based literacy approaches frequently invited participation and rich meaning-making, fewer studies attended to how such practices were sustained through ongoing or embedded triadic arrangements involving people, places, and texts. title: The dilemma of “Dahl dominance”: exploring the delights and difficulties of Dahl’s enduring presence in delivering the primary years English curriculum
text_snippet: The dilemma of “Dahl dominance”: exploring the delights and difficulties of Dahl’s enduring presence in delivering the primary years English curriculum Abstract Roald Dahl’s books have long captivated readers through imaginative stories and memorable characters, securing a persistent and prominent place in primary classrooms. The enduring popularity of Dahl’s works, however, raises pressing professional questions concerning the diversity, appropriateness, and alignment of children’s literature used to enact the primary years English curriculum. This article contributes to scholarship on text selection practices in primary English by addressing the documented dilemma of Dahl dominance , and the tensions it produces for curriculum enactment. Focusing on The Twits (Dahl & Blake, 1981), this article presents a critical literary analysis to examine how the text aligns with contemporary curricular and pedagogical responsibilities. To situate this analysis, the article draws primarily on scholarship examining Roald Dahl’s work within children’s literature studies, as well as research on inherited classroom canons and teachers’ reading repertoires. title: “Insufficiently Korean” to strategic meaning-maker: textual transpositioning and multilingual identity work
text_snippet: “Insufficiently Korean” to strategic meaning-maker: textual transpositioning and multilingual identity work Abstract Educational institutions continue to position multilingual capabilities as deficiencies requiring remediation rather than strategic resources deserving recognition and nurturing. Current translanguaging approaches focus primarily on spontaneous spoken interactions, leaving unexamined the sustained creative production through which multilingual writers develop strategic awareness of their complete linguistic repertoires. This paper introduces textual transpositioning as a framework for reconceptualising multilingual writing instruction. Drawing on a 6-month collaborative dialogue methodology, we examine how one multilingual author created Kimchi is for Everyone , a picturebook that orchestrates Korean and English resources without compartmentalisation. Through sustained dialogue, we analysed how strategic capabilities emerged through this creative process. title: Writing for well-being; The therapeutic power of the compositional process
text_snippet: Writing for well-being; The therapeutic power of the compositional process Abstract For more than a decade, concerns about falling standards of writing, measured against national assessment criteria, have reinforced a narrowly framed paradigm in the teaching of writing. Concurrently, evidence suggests that levels of children’s and young people’s psychological and emotional well-being have deteriorated, particularly during, and following, mass lockdowns caused by Covid − 19 viruses. Interview data from a small-scale study of primary student teachers who engaged in expressive journal writing during a literacy unit, suggests the act of writing under stress-free conditions can provide personal spaces for self-reflection, leading to ameliorative states of thinking and feeling about the self. Echoing Yagelski’s (2012) call for a ‘revolution in writing’, these findings suggest the case for radical change to a pedagogy of writing that incorporates the acquisition of technical skills within an approach that allows for personal expression, agency and well-being. It is posited that the re-framing of writing as process rather than as an essentially ‘skills-based’ product might help to both improve students’ mental and emotional well-being, as well as their writing.

title: Increasing writing engagement in a South Australian year two classroom
text_snippet: Increasing writing engagement in a South Australian year two classroom Abstract This participatory action research study explores how targeted instructional strategies can enhance writing engagement among Year 2 students in a South Australian primary classroom. Framing writing engagement as a multidimensional construct—affective, behavioural, cognitive, and social—the study investigates the impact of a co-designed, multimodal narrative writing unit integrating student choice, authentic audiences, and collaborative opportunities. Over three months, observational data, modified writing engagement surveys, and student interviews were collected to assess engagement during traditional teacher-directed writing tasks and the multimodal project. Findings revealed consistently high behavioural engagement across contexts, but significantly greater affective engagement—both positive and negative—during multimodal video creation sessions. Students reported increased enjoyment and perceived authenticity in the multimodal project, despite describing it as more cognitively demanding. title: The ‘how long’ question: language learning trajectories of EAL learners in NSW schools
text_snippet: The ‘how long’ question: language learning trajectories of EAL learners in NSW schools Abstract Nearly one quarter of students in Australian schools are learning English as an additional language (EAL). However, despite international research, and one Australian study, there is limited direct evidence of the length of time required for EAL students in Australia to develop the English necessary to access the curriculum in the same ways as their non-EAL peers. This article reports on outcomes from a large-scale project that investigated this issue. The project involved analysis of NAPLAN results in reading and writing from EAL students in NSW public schools from 2014 to 2022, and was supported by NSW Department of Education. The article outlines the challenges and methodological decisions involved in undertaking research of this nature, including the use of propensity score matching to control for the possibility of confounding factors. Results from the research confirm the overall length of time required for EAL students to develop high levels of academic English; they provide evidence of students’ progress in academic writing in comparison to reading; and they show the impact of students’ different starting levels on their overall progression in academic English. title: Liminal childhoods and the refusal of order: reading Alice, Chhuti, HaJaBaRaLa, and contemporary Australian children’s literature
text_snippet: Liminal childhoods and the refusal of order: reading Alice, Chhuti, HaJaBaRaLa, and contemporary Australian children’s literature Abstract This paper brings together five children’s texts— Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (Carroll), Chhuti (Tagore), HaJaBaRaLa (Ray), The Lost Girl (Kwaymullina), and My Two Blankets (Kobald & Blackwood)—to theorise childhood as a site of liminality, affective disruption, and epistemic resistance. Their breadth is deliberate: placing colonial, postcolonial, and multicultural works in conversation affirms a pluriversal frame that resists narrow canons and positions children’s literature as both critical and creative pedagogy. Drawing on poststructuralist (Deleuze, Butler, Nietzsche) and postcolonial (Bhabha, Spivak, Nandy) frameworks, the analysis explores how these texts unsettle normative binaries—adult/child, English/Other, coloniser/colonised—and reimagine children not as incomplete beings but as relational, agentic figures navigating cultural tension and world-making. From Alice’s linguistic absurdity and Phatik’s emotional dislocation to Ray’s subversive nonsense, the canonical works interrogate adult rationality and colonial logics through motifs of play, silence, and refusal, which reverberate in contemporary Australian picturebooks where Kwaymullina’s The Lost Girl fore

title: Multiliteracies pedagogy: teachers’ interactive and reflexive positionings in EAL classrooms
text_snippet: Multiliteracies pedagogy: teachers’ interactive and reflexive positionings in EAL classrooms Abstract The increasingly culturally and linguistically diverse nature of the educational landscape in Australia requires teachers to implement classroom practice that responds to the changes, demands and challenges of a diverse and highly technologised world. In this study, it is suggested that implementing multiliteracies classroom practice is a relational and situated process in which English as an Additional Language (EAL) teachers draw on their perspective of EAL students and themselves. Informed by positioning theory and the personal interpretive framework, the study examined the positioning that EAL teachers ascribed to EAL students (interactive positioning) and to themselves (reflexive positioning) in relation to the implementation of multiliteracies pedagogy. Analysis of data from individual interviews with six EAL teachers shows that the teachers positioned EAL learners as having diverse learning styles and needs and as users of technology.
